explain.title: Patterns
explain.body: A mathematical pattern is a predictable arrangement of numbers, shapes, or symbols that follows a specific rule or relationship. For example, in 1, 4, 7, 10, 13, each term is found by adding 3 to the previous term.

explain.title: Structures and relationships
explain.body: A mathematical structure is a collection of items or objects, along with particular relationships defined among them. Looking for how parts repeat or connect helps us understand the structure. We can also establish a relationship between two sets when there is a correspondence between the numbers of these sets.

explain.title: Sets and their forms
explain.body: A set is described as a well-defined collection of distinct objects, numbers or elements, so that we may be able to decide whether the object belongs to the collection or not. A set can be described in words, by listing its elements in tabular (roster) form, or by stating a shared property in set-builder form.

explain.title: Membership and subsets
explain.body: The symbol ∈ means that an element belongs to a set, and ∉ means it does not belong. If every element of A is an element of B, then A is a subset of B. A proper subset is not equal to the larger set.

explain.title: Empty set and power set
explain.body: The empty set has no elements, while a singleton set has one element. The power set of a set S denoted by P(S) is the set containing all the possible subsets of S. If S has m elements, its power set has 2^m elements.

mistakes: Do not confuse {0}, which has one element, with ∅, which has no elements.
Do not confuse equal sets, which have the same elements, with equivalent sets, which have the same number of elements.
Do not forget that a power set includes the empty set and the original set.
Count an element that is itself a set as one element; for example, {a, {b, c}} has two elements.
In set-builder notation, include the correct number set and the correct bounds.
Remember that a proper subset cannot be equal to the original set.

example.question:
EXAMPLE 6: A survey of 130 customers in a shopping mall was conducted in which they were asked about buying preferences.

The survey result showed the following statistics:

- 57 customers bought garments
- 50 customers bought cosmetics
- 46 customers bought electronics
- 31 customers purchased both garments and cosmetics
- 25 customers purchased both garments and electronics
- 21 customers purchased both cosmetics and electronics
- 12 customers purchased all three products i.e. garments, cosmetics, and electronics.

(a) How many of the customers bought at least one of the products: garments, cosmetics or electronics?

explain.title: Union and intersection
explain.body: The union A ∪ B contains elements in A or B, including elements in both. The intersection A ∩ B contains only elements that belong to both sets. Your textbook defines the union as “The union of two sets A and B, denoted by A∪B, is the set of all elements which belong to A or B.” It defines the intersection as “The intersection of two sets A and B, denoted by A ∩ B, is the set of all elements that belong to both A and B.”

explain.title: Difference and complement
explain.body: A − B keeps elements in A but not in B, so in general A − B ≠ B − A. The complement A′ contains elements of the universal set U that are not in A. Your textbook defines the difference as “The difference between the sets A and B denoted by A−B, consists of all the elements that belong to A but do not belong to B.” It defines the complement as “The complement of a set A, denoted by A' or A^c relative to the universal set U is the set of all elements of U, which do not belong to A.”

explain.title: Disjoint and overlapping sets
explain.body: Your textbook defines disjoint sets this way: “If the intersection of two sets is the empty set, the sets are said to be disjoint.” It defines overlapping sets this way: “If the intersection of two sets is non-empty but neither is a subset of the other, the sets are called overlapping sets.”

explain.title: Counting elements
explain.body: Your textbook defines cardinality as “The cardinality of a set is defined as the total number of elements of a set.” For two sets, n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B). For three sets, subtract the pairwise intersections and then add the triple intersection.

explain.title: De Morgan’s Laws
explain.body: The complement of a union is the intersection of the complements: (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′. The complement of an intersection is the union of the complements: (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′.

mistakes: Do not confuse ∪ (or) with ∩ (and).
Do not count a shared element twice when finding a union; subtract the intersection.
Do not assume A − B equals B − A; set difference is not commutative.
When finding a complement, use the stated universal set U; elements outside U cannot be included.
For three sets, subtract all three pairwise intersections and add the triple intersection once.
In a Venn diagram, pairwise intersection counts may include the central triple intersection unless the question explicitly says “only.”

explain.title: Relations and ordered pairs
explain.body: Mathematically, a relation is any set of ordered pairs. The first elements make the domain; the second elements make the range. For example, if r = {(1, 4), (2, 3)}, then Dom r = {1, 2} and Ran r = {4, 3}.

explain.title: What makes a relation a function?
explain.body: A function is a relation from A to B whose domain is A and whose ordered pairs do not have equal first elements. In other words, each input has one output. Different inputs may still have the same output.

explain.title: Types of functions
explain.body: An into function has Range f ⊂ B and Range f ≠ B. An onto function has Range f = B. A bijective function is both one-one and onto.

explain.title: Finding function values and constants
explain.body: To find f(k), replace every x in the function rule with k. If a rule contains unknown constants, substitute the given function values to form equations, then solve them together.

explain.title: Linear and quadratic functions
explain.body: The function {(x, y) | y = mx + c} is called a linear function because its graph is a straight line. The function {(x, y) | y = ax² + bx + c} is called a quadratic function.

mistakes: Mixing up domain and range: the domain uses first elements and the range uses second elements.
Forgetting that the relation must use ordered pairs from the given Cartesian product.
Calling a relation a function even when one input is paired with two different outputs.
Assuming a function must be onto; an into function can leave elements of B unused.
Forgetting brackets around a negative input before squaring, such as writing −4² instead of (−4)².
When finding unknown constants, stopping after finding one constant or making an arithmetic error when substituting back.
Giving only the final answer in a multi-step question and missing marks for the equations and working.

explain.title: Set notation and listing
explain.body: A set-builder description tells you which elements belong in a set. To write a set in tabular form, list its members inside braces. Check the number system and any restrictions in the description.

explain.title: Set operations
explain.body: A ∪ B contains elements in A or B or both. A ∩ B contains elements common to both. A − B contains elements in A but not in B. A′ contains elements in the universal set U that are not in A.

explain.title: Counting unions
explain.body: For two sets, n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B). Subtract the intersection because it was counted once in each set.

explain.title: Three-set counting
explain.body: For three sets, add the three individual counts, subtract the three pairwise intersections, then add the triple intersection. This corrects the repeated counting.

explain.title: Cartesian products and functions
explain.body: The number of ordered pairs in A × B is n(A) × n(B). To evaluate a function, replace x with the input value and simplify using the correct order of operations.

mistakes: Counting shared elements twice when finding a union.
Forgetting that a complement is taken relative to the universal set U.
Confusing A − B with B − A; set difference is not generally reversible.
For a Cartesian product, adding the set sizes instead of multiplying them.
Substituting a function input incorrectly, especially when the input is negative or a fraction.
In three-set inclusion-exclusion, forgetting to add the triple intersection back.

notes.title: Sets and power sets
notes.explanation: A power set lists every possible subset of a set. Include the empty set and the original set.
notes.simple: A set is a collection of different items. A subset is made from some or all of those items; the power set gathers all the subsets.
examples: If a set has 2 elements, its power set has 2² = 4 elements.
steps: Count the elements in the original set: n(S) = 2.
Use n(P(S)) = 2^m, where m is the number of elements in S.
notes.checkQuestion: How many elements are in the power set of a set with 2 elements?

notes.title: Operations on Sets and Counting Overlaps
notes.answer: For two sets, n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B). For three sets, add the three set sizes, subtract the three pairwise intersections, then add the triple intersection.
notes.explanation: Union collects elements in either set; intersection collects elements in both. For counting, add the set sizes and subtract overlaps that were counted more than once. For three sets, add the triple intersection back after subtracting the pairwise intersections.
notes.simple: Union means everything in either set. Intersection means what the sets share. When counting a union, subtract the shared elements so they are not counted twice.
steps: Write the set sizes and the size of their union.
Use n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).
Rearrange to find the intersection: n(A ∩ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∪ B).

notes.title: Relations and functions
notes.answer: A function is a relation in which no two ordered pairs have equal first elements.
notes.explanation: A relation is a set of ordered pairs. A function is a special relation where each input has exactly one output. To find a function value, substitute the given input for x. To find unknown constants, substitute the given function values and solve the resulting equations.
notes.simple: A relation pairs things up. In a function, each input is paired with only one output.
steps: For a relation, list the ordered pairs that satisfy the given condition.
The domain is the set of first elements in the pairs.
The range is the set of second elements in the pairs.
For a function value, replace x with the given number and simplify.
For unknown constants, substitute the given function values, form equations, and solve.

quiz.stem: Which statement best describes a mathematical pattern?
options: A predictable arrangement that follows a rule or relationship
A collection that must contain numbers only
A list with no repeated rule
A shape that has no parts
rationales: Correct: a mathematical pattern follows a rule or relationship.
Wrong: patterns can involve shapes or symbols as well as numbers.
Wrong: a pattern is predictable and follows a rule.
Wrong: a pattern may use shapes, but this is not its definition.

quiz.stem: What is a singleton set?
options: A set with exactly one element
A set with infinitely many elements
rationales: Correct: a singleton set has only one element.
Wrong: a set with no elements is an empty set.
Wrong: the definition does not require infinitely many elements.
Wrong: elements of a set need not be numbers.

quiz.stem: Which of these is a singleton set?
rationales: Correct: {0} has one element, namely 0.
Wrong: ∅ has no elements.
Wrong: {} denotes the empty set and has no elements.
Wrong: the set of natural numbers has more than one element.

quiz.stem: When are two sets equal?
options: They have exactly the same elements.
They have the same number of elements.
They have no elements in common.
One must have more elements than the other.
rationales: Correct: equal sets contain exactly the same elements.
Wrong: having the same number of elements describes equivalent sets.
Wrong: equal sets must have all the same elements, not none in common.
Wrong: equal sets have the same elements and therefore the same number of elements.

quiz.stem: Which is the set-builder form of {1, 2, 3}?
options: A = {x | x is a natural number less than 4}
A is the set of natural numbers less than 4
rationales: Wrong: this is roster form, listing the elements.
Correct: it uses a variable and a property that describes the elements.
Wrong: this describes the set in words, which is descriptive form.
Wrong: this describes all integers, not just 1, 2, and 3.

quiz.stem: If every element of A is in B and B has at least one element not in A, which notation shows that A is a proper subset of B?
rationales: Correct: A ⊂ B denotes a proper subset.
Wrong: A = B would mean the sets have exactly the same elements.
Wrong: A ~ B means the sets have the same number of elements.
Wrong: ∉ means is not an element of.

quiz.stem: If a finite set S has m elements, how many elements does its power set have?
rationales: Correct: the number of elements of P(S) is 2^m.
Wrong: m² is not the power-set counting rule.
Wrong: 2m is not the power-set counting rule.
Wrong: m + 2 is not the power-set counting rule.

quiz.stem: What rule generates each term of the Fibonacci sequence described in your textbook?
rationales: Correct: each term is obtained by adding the previous two terms.
Wrong: the described Fibonacci rule uses addition, not multiplication.
Wrong: adding 3 is the rule for a different numerical pattern in the section.
Wrong: the described rule adds the previous two terms.

quiz.stem: Which statement describes the union A ∪ B?
options: Elements in A or B, or both
Elements in both A and B only
Elements in A but not B
Elements outside both A and B
rationales: Correct: the union contains every element belonging to A or B, including shared elements.
Incorrect: this describes the intersection A ∩ B.
Incorrect: this describes the difference A − B.
Incorrect: this describes the complement of A ∪ B in the universal set.

quiz.stem: If A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {2, 3, 4, 5}, what is A ∩ B?
rationales: Correct: 2 and 3 are the elements that belong to both sets.
Incorrect: this is A ∪ B, not the intersection.
Incorrect: 1, 4 and 5 do not belong to both sets.
Incorrect: 4 and 5 are in B only, not in A.

quiz.stem: Which expression gives the elements that belong to A but do not belong to B?
rationales: Correct: A − B contains elements in A that are not in B.
Incorrect: A ∩ B contains elements in both sets.
Incorrect: A ∪ B contains elements in either set.
Incorrect: A′ contains elements of the universal set that are not in A.

quiz.stem: Which equality gives the complement of A relative to U?
rationales: Correct: the complement contains elements of U that are not in A.
Incorrect: U ∩ A gives A when A is a subset of U.
Incorrect: A − U is empty when A is a subset of U.
